title: Indicators of Compromise: Reading the Traces

blocks.text: An indicator is not a conclusion. It is an observable fact that becomes meaningful when correlated with context, a baseline, and a timeline.
IOC and IOA: Artifact and Behavior

An **IOC** (Indicator of Compromise) is an artifact observed after the fact: a malware hash, a command-and-control IP address, a domain, a registry key. An **IOA** (Indicator of Attack) describes a **behavior**: a process launching encoded PowerShell, an abnormal outbound connection, a sudden privilege escalation. IOCs are static and easy to block but quickly obsolete; IOAs are more durable but harder to detect.

blocks.field: Often exchanged via threat intelligence feeds (STIX/TAXII). An IOC alone proves nothing: it must be correlated.
Behavioral, aligned with MITRE ATT&CK. More resilient to changes in attacker infrastructure.

blocks.text: The Twelve Official Indicators

head: Indicator
What Is Observed
Concrete Example
rows: Repeated connection to a blocklisted IP
DNS resolution to an algorithmically generated domain
Abnormal process, misleading name, unusual path
Discrepancy between system time and logs
Abnormal CPU, memory, disk, or network usage
Cryptomining: 100% CPU on an idle server
Credentials or keys in a binary or script
Base64 password in a config file
Two active sessions for the same account
Two distinct IP addresses, same token

blocks.title: Impossible Travel and Concurrent Sessions
blocks.text: The two look similar but do not say the same thing. **Impossible travel**: two authentications too far apart in time and space for physical travel. **Concurrent sessions**: the same account active from two locations at the same time. Both suggest credential or token theft, not necessarily a different attack.
Why Correlation Changes Everything

One account lockout might be a user who forgot their password. Twenty lockouts across ten accounts in five minutes, followed by a successful login from an unknown IP, tell a different story: **password spraying** or a distributed brute-force attack. Analysis means moving from the isolated event to the **sequence**.

**Log manipulation** is a particularly serious indicator: an attacker who clears logs is trying to destroy evidence. Watch for log-clearing events, audit service restarts, audit policy changes, and logs that "skip" a time period.

blocks.q: An analyst sees an account log in from Paris at 09:00 and then from Singapore at 09:20. Which indicator is most directly involved?
blocks.explain: The Paris–Singapore trip in 20 minutes is physically impossible. This suggests credential or session theft. You must then check whether these are two concurrent sessions, a VPN, or a proxy before concluding compromise.

items: IOC = artifact (hash, IP, domain); IOA = behavior (process, sequence).
The twelve official indicators must be recognized in a scenario, not just recited.
An isolated indicator is not proof: correlation and timeline make the analysis.
Log clearing is an indicator of concealment, hence a strong signal.

title: Malware and Network Attacks: Recognizing the Modus Operandi

blocks.text: A malware's name often describes its propagation method or its effect. Knowing how to distinguish a worm from a virus, or a Trojan from a rootkit, changes the response required.
The Ten Malware Families

items: **Ransomware**: encrypts data and demands payment. Indicators: modified extensions, ransom notes, massive file access, shadow copy deletion.
**Trojan**: poses as legitimate software. It does not infect other files: it opens a door.
**Worm**: spreads on its own over the network without user action. Indicators: rapid internal scans, connection spikes.
**Spyware**: collects information (browsing, keystrokes, screen). Indicators: regular outbound traffic, sensor access.
**Adware**: displays ads, often bundled with free software. Indicators: redirects, browser extensions.
**Virus**: attaches to a file or boot sector and spreads upon execution. Indicators: modified files, abnormal size.
**Rootkit**: hides compromise at the kernel or firmware level. Indicators: discrepancies between tools, invisible processes.
**Keylogger**: records keystrokes. Indicators: keyboard hook, local log file, periodic exfiltration.
**Logic bomb**: triggers an action on a date or event. Indicators: conditional code, suspicious scheduled task.
**Fileless malware**: lives in memory, with no file on disk. Indicators: encoded PowerShell, process injection, WMI.

blocks.field: Relies on native tools (PowerShell, WMI, mshta, regsvr32): this is "living off the land". Signature-based antivirus is blind; EDR and behavioral telemetry are required.

blocks.title: Worm, Virus, Trojan: The Exact Distinction
blocks.text: A **worm** spreads on its own over the network. A **virus** needs a host (file, boot sector) and execution. A **Trojan** does not self-propagate: it tricks the user into running it. A **rootkit** does not propagate either: it hides. A question may combine terms; go back to the definition of propagation.
Network Attacks

head: Attack
Mechanism
Observable Indicator
rows: Massive inbound traffic, latency, connection exhaustion
Forcing TLS to a weak version
New MAC address, unknown DHCP, active port
Interface in promiscuous mode, unauthorized port mirror
IP, MAC, or DNS address spoofing
Injecting forged entries into a cache
Persistent incorrect DNS or ARP response

blocks.text: An **on-path attack** (formerly called man-in-the-middle) places the attacker between two parties. They can read, modify, or replay traffic. Without encryption, they see everything; with properly validated TLS, they only see ciphertext — hence the importance of certificate validation and not "clicking through the warning".

blocks.title: Exam Terminology
blocks.text: The books use **MITM** (man-in-the-middle). The SY0-801 objectives use **on-path attack**. On the exam, look for "on-path"; in the literature, "MITM" remains common.
Physical Attacks

**Tailgating** is following an authorized person without a badge. **Shoulder surfing** is reading over someone's shoulder (screen, keyboard, PIN). **Skimming** copies a payment card's magnetic stripe. **Forced entry** is physical break-in. Corresponding controls are mantraps, zone separation, privacy screens, and badge verification.

blocks.note: Kill Chain, MITM, lateral movement, alert severity

blocks.q: A server shows 100% CPU usage outside business hours, regular outbound traffic to an unknown IP, and no suspicious files on disk. Which hypothesis is most likely?
options: A classic virus attached to a system file
Fileless malware, possibly a cryptominer or in-memory implant
blocks.explain: The absence of files on disk, high CPU usage, and regular outbound traffic point to fileless malware (PowerShell, process injection) or a cryptominer. A virus would leave modified files; an inbound DDoS would saturate the network, not the CPU in this way.

items: Worm = autonomous propagation; virus = host + execution; Trojan = deception; rootkit = concealment.
Fileless = memory and native tools: EDR and telemetry take precedence over signatures.
On-path (MITM): interception; TLS validation is the key countermeasure.
Each network attack has an observable indicator: correlate traffic, logs, and configuration.

title: Social Engineering, Application Attacks, and Credential Attacks

blocks.text: The most effective attacks do not break cryptography: they convince a human, exploit unvalidated input, or reuse a stolen credential.
Social Engineering

head: Attack
Channel
Warning Sign
rows: Pressure, spoofed number, request for MFA code
Shortened link, package, fine, locked account
QR sticker on a terminal, payment link

blocks.field: The QR code bypasses email filters that analyze text and URLs. It is often placed on a payment terminal or embedded in a PDF.
AI-generated video or voice. Used for executive fraud and extortion. Verification via a second channel remains the best defense.

blocks.text: A **watering hole** is a variant: the attacker compromises a legitimate site frequented by the target (industry association, vendor portal) to infect its visitors. The indicator is a change in behavior of a trusted site, not a suspicious email.
Application Attacks

items: **Injection** (SQL, command, LDAP): unvalidated input is interpreted as code. Indicator: SQL errors, abnormal queries, `' OR 1=1`.
**Buffer overflow**: writing beyond allocated memory, causing a crash or execution. Indicator: repeated crashes, memory corruption.
**Replay**: replaying a valid request or token. Indicator: same request repeated, token reused outside its window.
**Privilege escalation**: moving from a standard account to an administrator account. Indicator: addition to a privileged group, elevated token.
**Forgery** (CSRF, request forgery): action executed on behalf of the user without their consent. Indicator: POST requests without an anti-CSRF token.
**Directory traversal**: accessing a file outside the intended directory via `../`. Indicator: requests containing `../` or `%2e%2e`.

blocks.title: Injection: The Principle Before the Name
blocks.text: Every injection relies on the same mistake: **mixing data and instructions**. The fix is structural (parameterized queries, strict validation, least privilege), not simple character filtering.
Credential Attacks

right.title: Password Spraying
points: Detection: distributed failures, same time window, same IP

blocks.text: **User enumeration** determines which accounts exist (different error messages, response times). **Replay** reuses a captured token or authentication. **MFA bypass** exploits push fatigue (repeated notifications), intercepted OTP, or a poorly protected reset flow.

head: Attack
What You See in Logs
Immediate Response
rows: Burst of failures on one account
Failures across many accounts, same IP
Repeated pushes, code approved out of context
Number matching, FIDO2 keys, account lock

blocks.q: An attacker tests the password `Summer2026!` on 300 different accounts, once each, in five minutes. What attack is this?
blocks.explain: A single password tried against many accounts at low frequency per account is password spraying. It bypasses per-account lockout and exploits password reuse. Brute force would concentrate attempts on one account.

items: Phishing, spear, whaling, vishing, smishing, quishing, deepfake: the channel and targeting change, not the principle.
Injection = data interpreted as instructions; the fix is structural.
Brute force = one account; spraying = one password across many accounts.
Responding to a credential attack starts with session invalidation and MFA hardening.
